extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science; historians of science
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains Kuhn-era criteria and standards for evaluating scientific theories, paradigm change, and historical interpretation of scientific practice. Focuses on semantic/taxonomic incommensurability, criteria for scientific progress, and methodological/naturalistic responses to Kuhn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning holism
rubrics_metrics.description: The meanings of terms are interrelated so that changing the meaning of one term results in changes in the meanings of related terms; the whole conceptual web must be shifted for a major theoretical transition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to support Kuhn's claim that shifts (e.g., from Newtonian to Einsteinian concepts) change networks of meaning so that direct translation or simple comparison of terms across paradigms is blocked; undercuts the idea that observation sentences are theory-neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomic incommensurability (lexical network change)
rubrics_metrics.description: A field is governed by a taxonomy and associated lexical network; significant scientific change alters the lexical network and thereby re-aligns the taxonomy so that terms of the old and new taxonomies are not inter-translatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn holds that changes to lexical networks during revolutions make certain translations impossible; this is presented as a core source of semantic incommensurability.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-overlap principle for taxonomies
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories in a taxonomy must be hierarchically organized: if two categories share members one must include the other; otherwise they are disjoint and cannot merely overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle rules out constructing an all-encompassing taxonomy that simultaneously contains both old and new taxonomic schemes, and helps explain how revolutions produce distinct, non-mergeable conceptual frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-dependence of observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational sentences and apparently observational terms are influenced by the theoretical context; observation is not theory-neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn uses this to argue that holism of theoretical meaning extends to observational language, blocking the escape route that would solve incommensurability by appealing to theory-neutral observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-language model of theoretical meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of a theoretical term is a product of (1) the relation of the theory/theories of which it is part to their observational consequences and (2) the role that the particular term plays within those theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was the standard positivist picture Kuhn challenged; it emphasizes that theoretical statements are not reducible to observational sentences and that theory provides meaning to theoretical terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for paradigm choice (community standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialist scientific communities have shared standards for evaluating proposed puzzle-solutions; choice of a new paradigm is based on solving important hitherto unsolved problems while preserving as much problem-solving power of the preceding paradigm as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn emphasizes community-held evaluative standards (not fixed rules) and that paradigms are accepted because of comparative problem-solving success and retention of useful legacy problem-solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anomalies as drivers of revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific revolutions arise when persistent anomalies accumulate that cannot be solved within the current paradigm, prompting the community to adopt a new paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn presents anomaly-accumulation as the typical route to revolution; critics point out important discoveries (e.g., DNA structure) can also initiate revolutionary change without the anomaly story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kuhnian criterion for scientific progress (evolutionary view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific progress consists in solving more and more detailed puzzles and increasing sophistication/specialization of the discipline; improvement is not measured by getting closer to a final truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn's Darwinian analogy yields a notion of genuine progress that is non-teleological: later science is 'better' in problem-solving capacities and specialization but not necessarily nearer to an absolute truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements/criteria for being 'science' (positivist, Popperian, Kuhnian contrasts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different accounts set different standards: positivists demand verifiability via predictive success; Popper demands potential falsifiability; Kuhn requires domination by a paradigm that generates distinctive puzzles and criteria for assessing solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrast is used to show why Kuhn's picture can more readily accommodate fields (e.g., some social sciences) that lack precise predictive power but may have paradigm-like puzzle-solving structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedean-platform requirement for cross-era comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: To compare theories from older and more recent periods for 'nearness to the truth' one would need a perspective external to each era (an 'Archimedean platform'), which Kuhn thinks we lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to motivate skepticism about our ability to know that later theories are closer to truth; realist replies appeal to other strategies (e.g., referential continuity, externalist epistemology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Referentialist defense criteria (causal theories of reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: If theoretical terms secure reference to the same worldly entities across theory change (via causal or causal-descriptive theories of reference), then comparison of theories with respect to truth-nearness remains possible despite semantic shifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard realist response to Kuhn: even if senses shift, shared reference can ground claims that later theories improve on earlier ones; the defense requires case-by-case argument for referential continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalized/externalist epistemic criterion for method adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: One may reject the requirement that methods be independent of particular perspectives; if a method is reliable in the relevant circumstances it can generate knowledge even if theory-laden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This response to Kuhn's Archimedean worry lets defenders of realism claim we can know that newer methods/theories are better if those methods are reliable, and science itself investigates and improves methods over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution of lexicons and synchronic isolation (specialization criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: As scientific specialties branch and their lexicons evolve, they become conceptually isolated (incommensurable) from one another; lexical evolution contributes to the fragmentation of disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underlies Kuhn's later view that incommensurability isolates communities synchronically as well as diachronically, especially through hierarchical/no-overlap taxonomic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestalt-switch analogy for world-change
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradigm change is likened to a gestalt perceptual switch (e.g., seeing the duck-rabbit alternately), suggesting a radical change in how the world is experienced without implying literal constructivism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn used the analogy to illustrate perceptual/interpretive change but denied committing to strong constructivism; it's offered as both metaphor and possible psychological model, though its applicability is debated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical interpretation criterion (avoid presentism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical assessment of earlier scientists should interpret their work in light of the puzzles and conceptual resources available to them rather than judging by current standards; apparent backwardness can be a distortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn's historical studies (e.g., Copernicus, Planck) show how presentist readings exaggerate differences and underappreciate the rationality of past practitioners operating within their problem contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five constitutive scientific values (Kuhn's claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kuhn ascribes five values to all science which he regards as constitutive of scientific practice and judgment (the text notes these as constitutive though the specific five are not listed in this chunk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn argues an enterprise with different values could exist but would not be science; these shared values both guide normal scientific judgment and provide the standards by which paradigms and puzzle-solutions are assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalistic/developmental bases for conceptual change
rubrics_metrics.description: Kuhn appeals to developmental psychology and biological evolution to explain conceptual change: innate object-recognition mechanisms and language acquisition shape lexical/contact principles (e.g., no-overlap) that underlie scientific taxonomy changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports a naturalistic account of incommensurability and conceptual change, suggesting cognitive and evolutionary roots for lexicon evolution and constraints on taxonomic restructuring.
